extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of folklore, antiquarian scholars, and comparative mythology researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Comparative-historical analysis of the origins, attributes, and transformations of European fairy/elf traditions, tracing influences (Oriental, Gothic, chivalric, classical, Christian, sixteenth-century imagination) and illustrative tales. The page functions as an academic/antiquarian survey of folkloric motifs and their transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scandinavian duergar/elves attributes (Torfaeus / Einar Gudmund account)
rubrics_metrics.description: These beings are creatures of God, consisting, like human beings, of a body and rational soul; that they are of different sexes, and capable of producing children, and subject to all human affections, as sleeping and waking, laughing and crying, poverty and wealth; and that they possess cattle, and other effects, and are obnoxious to death, like other mortals. The females of this race are capable of procreating with mankind; one bore a child to an inhabitant of Iceland, and claimed the privilege of baptism, depositing the infant at the gate of the church-yard together with a goblet of gold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording cited from Torfaeus (preface to Hrolf Kraka) and a dissertation by Einar Gudmund; footnote suggests possible historical basis (oppressed Fins driven to mountains becoming supernatural duergar). Examples: Hervarar Saga enchanted sword; Skoffhung.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplanders' subterranean people characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Subterranean people in Lapland: resembling men in general appearance, manner of existence, and habits of life, yet far excelling the Laplanders in perfection of nature, felicity of situation, and skill in mechanical arts; they engage in banquets, dances, magical ceremonies, and intimate commerce of gallantry, share feasts in elfin caverns with wine and tobacco, and conduct mortal guests safely back to their tents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account credited to 'Jessens, de Lapponibus.' Notes that after partial conversion these beings were confounded with devils and magicians; local boast of intercourse persists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feroe Froddenskemen / under-ground people lore
rubrics_metrics.description: Froddenskemen (under-ground people) inhabit interior recesses of mountains entered by invisible passages; like Fairies, they are supposed to steal human beings. Examples include Jonas Soideman (kept by spirits in a mountain for seven years) and another man carried away who returned after rejecting a beautiful woman's entreaties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific motifs: invisible entrances, abduction and return, temptation by beautiful female spirits, and local naming of sea-beans as 'the Fairie's kidney'. Source: Debes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six main causes modifying elfin/fiary superstition
rubrics_metrics.description: The rudiments of elfin superstition are modified by (1) traditions of the east; (2) the wreck and confusion of the Gothic mythology; (3) the tales of chivalry; (4) the fables of classical antiquity; (5) the influence of the Christian religion; (6) the creative imagination of the sixteenth century.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author proposes to examine each cause's effect on popular belief; these six headings act as an organizing rubric for tracing changes in fairy lore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oriental (Persian/Arabic) influence and the 'Peri' model
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'Fairy' (Faërie) likely derives from oriental origin (Persic 'Peri' via Arabic); Peris are described as gentle, amiable females, beneficent and beautiful, subsisting on odours of flowers, not malicious or deformed, and unlike Gothic fairies in character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Romances and troubadours adopted Peri-like figures (Mergian Banou → Morgue La Faye, Urgande La Deconnue, Fata Morgana). The Arabic/Persian transmission via crusaders and Moorish Spain is emphasized; Ouseley and Herbelot cited for examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: British fairies' conflation with hags, night-mares, and malicious spirits
rubrics_metrics.description: In Britain (especially Scotland) fairies retained diminutive, unamiable Gothic traits and absorbed attributes from other classes of spirits: abstraction of children formerly ascribed to night-mares or hags, water-spirits (dracae), and Lamiae; tales attribute nocturnal oppression, infant injury, and the carrying off of women and children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: legend of St Margaret, Gervase of Tilbury's Lamiae and Dracae, Heywood's characterization, Frisian 'witte wiven' tradition; notes that in Germany classes remain more distinct (Erl King ballads).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chivalric / martial influence on fairy character
rubrics_metrics.description: Chivalry endowed fairies with martial, knightly qualities: fairy-knights, aërial hosts (Milites Herlikini / Herleurini), military processions, nightly combats and justings; stories include Osbert's challenge and encounter with a spirit-knight, the Bohemian knight overthrown by a fairy host, and the Hellequin procession condemned to wander.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tales cited from Gervase of Tilbury and French romance (Richard sans Peur). Folkloric motifs: justing with a ghostly knight, recurring wounds that reopen on anniversaries, and the fern-seed vigil (St John's Eve) where seekers risk fairy assault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical antiquity's contribution (nymphs, Diana, tutelary deities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical fables lent pastoral and mythological features to fairies: local tutelary deities, nymphs of woods/rivers/mountains, the Fairy Queen identified with Diana (Hecate) and other classical figures; popular tradition sometimes equates fairy attendants with Diana's nymphs and assigns corresponding insignia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include transformations of the Fairy Queen into Habundia, Gyre-Carline/Nicneven; an anecdote of Vulcan and Cyclops appearing in Sicily (1536) and a Roman tale where a statue of Venus claims a man's ring. Sources include Delrius and Narratives from Italy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water-spirits (dracae) motifs and overlap with fairy lore
rubrics_metrics.description: Dracae/water-spirits are depicted as malevolent beings inhabiting rivers/lakes who inveigle women/children by appearing as floating golden rings or cups, carry them away to subterranean watery recesses, employ women as nurses for seven years, and occasionally permit return; Scottish variants substitute fairies for dracae with caverns instead of rivers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gervase's accounts and Heywood's verses cited; parallels drawn to modern Scottish tales. The motif of acquiring special sight (seeing dracae) after contact with serpent's grease ointment is noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief in subterranean palaces, invisible portals, and mountain-lake entrances
rubrics_metrics.description: Common motif: mountains and high hills with bottomless lakes or pits leading to subterranean palaces of spirits, invisible porches, and audible subterranean murmurs (children's cries, music). Tales include Peter de Cabinam's daughter taken after a rash wish, a swine-herd descending into a pit to recover a sow, and ringing invisible bells at Laikibraine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gervase of Tilbury and other chroniclers provide multiple continental and British examples; wells/pits on hilltops commonly believed to be entrances to fairy habitations; motif widespread across Europe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motif of enchanted objects and 'luck' from fairy spoils (horns, goblets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fairy banquets sometimes yield enchanted drinking vessels or horns that confer good fortune if taken safely across running water; famous examples include a goblet presented to Henry I. and the 'luck of Edenhall' goblet preserved at Edenhall with the prophecy 'If this glass do break or fall, Farewell the luck of Edenhall!'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associated folkloric test: seize fairy cup/horn at a festival and carry it across a running stream; risks include losing fortune if the vessel is broken. Cited sources: Gervase, local English/Scottish traditions, Burlesque ballads.
